analysis.title: U.S. Data Center Capacity: Your seat is skewing your numbers. Five ways to forecast DC capacity (and our definitive view)
key_insights: Bernstein surveyed 63 forecasts from 40 sources and found a 2030 U.S. data center capacity spread of 59 to 186 GW. The note says the disagreement comes mostly from starting assumptions, units, timing conventions and the forecaster's place in the value chain, not from differences in end demand.

Bernstein's definitive estimate is 149 IT-GW of U.S. installed capacity by 2030, up from 33.7 IT-GW in 2025 (47.3 in 2026E, 67.0 in 2027E, 92.4 in 2028E, 120.5 in 2029E). It adds about 19 IT-GW (~25 facility GW) in 2027 and 25 IT-GW (~32 facility GW) in 2028.

The PM Summary text says the most reasonable outcome is ~160 IT-GW by 2030 (more than 4.5x 2025 levels) and cites a ~60 to 180+ GW industry range. The front page and Exhibit 1 give 149 IT-GW (149.2) and a 59 to 186 GW range, so the document is internally inconsistent. The 149 figure matches the exhibits.

Site-based method (infrastructure and REIT seat): uses the Aterio project database with completion and delay assumptions. It gives 134.5 to 167.2 IT-GW by 2030, base 142.3. Bernstein calls it the most actionable method for the next several years. Visibility fades beyond a few years, and credible GW is only about 35% of the total pipeline across all stages.

Incremental growth rate method (industrials seat): projects growth in annual capacity additions. It gives 124.3 to 242.4 IT-GW by 2030, base 161.0. It is highly sensitive to the starting point and growth assumptions and is not tied to identifiable projects. The base case is the highest of the five.

Hyperscaler-capex method (technology seat): converts capex into capacity. Total hyperscaler capex runs $466 (2025) to $856 (2026E) to $1,166 (2027E) and $1,269 (2030E), with 85% allocated to data centers. It gives a 2030 base of 151.5 IT-GW, range 115.1 to 195.3. Bernstein notes that capex is not capacity, and that disclosures vary widely and none give clear capacity breakdowns.
Server-based method (semis seat), built on David Dai's AI server power model: gives 148.6 IT-GW base by 2030, range 137.1 to 160.1. Timing and refresh-cycle assumptions are the main sources of error.

Craft labor ceiling (Chad Dillard): framed as a feasibility ceiling, not a demand forecast. It gives 142.4 IT-GW base by 2030, range 119.9 to 203.8. It is one of the more conservative methods alongside site-based.

Bernstein anchors 2025 capacity at 35 IT-GW (33.7 in the exhibits), counting only active data centers in its pipeline data. Credible outside estimates run from 30 to 80 GW. Bernstein says the starting point should perhaps be closer to 45 GW but keeps the source historicals so the incremental numbers are not distorted.

A GW is not a GW. IT-GW (critical IT load after a PUE haircut) is used by tech and data center analysts. Facility or nameplate GW is used by electricals, industrials and power analysts. Bernstein converts with a PUE assumption of 1.3 in 2026, trending gently down. Facility-GW base cases for 2030 range from 182.3 (site-based) to 206.0 (incremental growth).

Forecasts have been revised up almost uniformly. McKinsey raised its 2030 forecast by 258% between 2025 and 2026, BCG by 155% and EPRI by 99%. Bernstein says its own numbers have also ballooned since its early-2026 global supply and demand model, and that it changed its sourcing and research methodology.

Timing differs across the value chain. Equipment orders (cooling, power) front-run facility activation, and hardware follows activation by weeks to months. Bernstein counts IT-GW when a facility is fully energized and ready for hardware. Building takes at least 18 months and more typically a 3+ year planning process, extended by legislation in TX, PA and NY.

Incremental additions in the exhibits: the base-case average across methods is about 17 facility GW in 2026, 25 in 2027 and 32 in 2028. The range across methods is 16 to 20 in 2026, 22 to 29 in 2027 and 27 to 40 in 2028.

Positioning view: Bernstein favors companies with direct exposure to energized capacity growth over those whose outlook depends on the current pace of AI adoption. It says the market is supply constrained and new supply is absorbed shortly after delivery. It sees the greatest risk where valuations assume the most aggressive capacity outcomes with no execution challenges or delays.

sector_views.sector: Data center developers and colocation providers
sector_views.rationale: Bernstein expects strong demand and multi-year revenue visibility in its base case. The market is supply constrained, and new supply is often absorbed shortly after delivery.
The note lists them among infrastructure beneficiaries of a durable build cycle. Equipment orders front-run facility activation.

sector_views.sector: Companies whose valuations assume the most aggressive capacity outcomes
sector_views.rationale: The greatest risk is where valuations assume aggressive capacity outcomes with no execution challenges or delays. No names are identified.

risk_factors: Valuations that already assume the most aggressive capacity outcomes materialize without execution challenges or delays.

Some data centers will be delayed for regulatory, construction or business reasons, and others will never convert from announcement to operation. Only about 35% of the total pipeline is judged credible.
Hyperscalers may be over-ordering and building in a natural failure rate on construction projects.
Craft labor shortages, power infrastructure, equipment availability and permitting can cap deployment.
Increasing state legislation (TX, PA, NY) is lengthening planning timelines.
Forecast uncertainty is high: the 2025 starting base is disputed (30 to 80 GW), and results are sensitive to growth-rate, PUE, capex-to-capacity and hardware refresh assumptions.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 shows Bernstein's average base case U.S. capacity rising from 33.7 IT-GW in 2025 to 149.2 IT-GW in 2030E.
Exhibit 2 compares five method base cases for 2030E: site-based 142.3, incremental growth 161.0, hyperscale capex 151.5, server-based 148.6 and craft labor 142.4 IT-GW.
Exhibit 3 shows incremental facility GW by methodology, with average adds of 17 (2026E), 25 (2027E) and 32 (2028E) and ranges of 16-20, 22-29 and 27-40.
Exhibit 6 shows site-based facility GW in 2030E of 172.1 (low, 9-month delay), 182.2 (base, 6-month delay) and 214.0 (high, on schedule).
Exhibit 13 lists annual hyperscaler capex by company, 2025 to 2030E.

tension_points.bull_case: Incremental-growth and hyperscaler-capex methods give base cases of 161 and 152 IT-GW, with highs of 242 and 195. Demand exceeds available capacity in many regions, hyperscaler capex runs from $856 in 2026E to $1,166 in 2027E, and new supply is absorbed shortly after delivery.
tension_points.bear_case: Site-based and craft-labor methods give bases of 142 IT-GW, and the site-based low is 134.5. Only about 35% of the total pipeline is judged credible, projects can be delayed or cancelled, and labor, power, equipment and permitting can cap deployment.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The report does not give a numeric trigger. It names bottlenecks (craft labor, power infrastructure, equipment availability, permitting) and project delays or cancellations as the conditions that would cap capacity below the growth-rate and capex cases. It names the greatest risk as valuations that assume aggressive capacity outcomes with no execution challenges or delays.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers account for most capacity across self-builds and colo, and following their capex plans connects end demand to capacity.
tension_points.bear_case: Capex is not capacity. A dollar spent on accelerators creates less physical capacity than a dollar spent on facility construction. Some believe hyperscalers are over-ordering and building in a natural failure rate on projects.

theme_stances.key_argument: Whatever the method, the range of outcomes supports a durable infrastructure build cycle because the market is supply constrained and new capacity is absorbed after delivery.
theme_stances.evidence: ownership of, or exposure to, energized capacity remains particularly valuable

theme_stances.key_argument: Differences in starting point, units, timing and value-chain seat explain most of the spread between forecasts, and no single framework is complete.
theme_stances.evidence: Each framework captures a valid piece of the puzzle, but none offers a complete picture
